content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, a 'sign' (Hebrew 'oth, Greek semeion) is understood as a visible act, event, or object that points beyond itself to God's presence, power, and purpose — most characteristically a miraculous work that authenticates God's messenger and reveals divine identity. The paradigmatic usage is in John's Gospel, where Jesus' miracles are called 'signs' precisely because their significance lies not in the wonder itself but in what they disclose about who Jesus is (his glory, messiahship, and divine sonship), calling observers to faith.","primary_basis":["John 2:11 (the first sign at Cana manifesting Jesus' glory)","John 20:30-31 (signs written 'that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ')","Exodus 4:1-9 and Exodus 7:3 (signs authenticating Moses before Israel and Pharaoh)","Deuteronomy 4:34; 6:22 ('signs and wonders' of the Exodus as God's self-revelation)","Isaiah 7:14 (the sign of Immanuel given to Ahaz)","Acts 2:22 (Jesus 'attested by God with mighty works and wonders and signs')","John 3:2 (Nicodemus: 'no one can do these signs unless God is with him')","Hebrews 2:3-4 (God bearing witness by signs and wonders)"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Covenant sign or seal: a physical marker God attaches to a covenant as a perpetual reminder and pledge — the rainbow, circumcision, and the Sabbath. In Reformed and Catholic theology this extends to the sacraments (baptism, Lord's Supper) as visible signs and seals of invisible grace, following Augustine's definition of a sacrament as a visible sign of an invisible reality (cf. Romans 4:11, circumcision as 'sign and seal').","basis":["Genesis 9:12-17 (rainbow as sign of the covenant)","Genesis 17:11 (circumcision as sign of the covenant)","Exodus 31:13-17 (Sabbath as a sign between God and Israel)","Romans 4:11 (circumcision as a sign and seal of righteousness by faith)","Ezekiel 20:12,20 (Sabbath as sign)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Eschatological or apocalyptic indicator: 'signs of the times' and cosmic signs preceding the end — celestial disturbances, wars, false christs, and the 'sign of the Son of Man' — read as markers of Christ's return and the close of the age. This usage dominates prophecy-focused and dispensational teaching.","basis":["Matthew 24:3,30 ('what will be the sign of your coming?'; 'the sign of the Son of Man')","Luke 21:11,25 (signs in sun, moon, and stars)","Matthew 16:3 (interpreting the signs of the times)","Joel 2:30-31 / Acts 2:19 (wonders in heaven, signs on earth)","Revelation 12:1,3; 15:1 (great signs in heaven)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Sign as warning, judgment, or occasion of unbelief: demands for signs are portrayed negatively as faithless testing of God; the only sign given a wicked generation is the 'sign of Jonah' (Christ's death and resurrection, and implicitly a call to repentance under threat of judgment). Also false signs performed by deceivers.","basis":["Matthew 12:38-40; 16:1-4 (an evil generation seeks a sign; the sign of Jonah)","1 Corinthians 1:22 ('Jews demand signs')","John 4:48 ('unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe')","2 Thessalonians 2:9 and Matthew 24:24 (false signs and wonders of deceivers)","Mark 8:11-12 (no sign given to this generation)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Prophetic sign-act: symbolic actions performed by prophets (and by prophets' own lives or children) as enacted messages of coming judgment or salvation — e.g., Isaiah walking naked, Ezekiel's dramatizations, Hosea's marriage; the prophet himself as a sign to the people.","basis":["Isaiah 8:18 ('I and the children the LORD has given me are signs')","Isaiah 20:3 (Isaiah's nakedness as a sign against Egypt)","Ezekiel 4:1-3; 12:6,11; 24:24,27 ('Ezekiel shall be a sign to you')","Hosea 1:2-9 (Hosea's marriage and children as enacted signs)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Confirmatory sign granted to individuals as assurance of God's word or calling (e.g., Gideon's fleece, the sign to Ahaz, the shepherds' sign of the manger) — a personal token verifying a specific promise rather than a public miracle.","basis":["Judges 6:36-40 (Gideon's fleece)","Exodus 3:12 (the sign given to Moses)","1 Samuel 10:1-9 (signs confirming Saul's anointing)","Luke 2:12 ('this will be a sign to you: a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths')","2 Kings 20:8-11 (the sign of the shadow for Hezekiah)"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Charismatic/Pentecostal reading emphasizing signs (with tongues, healing, and wonders) as ongoing marks accompanying believers and the gospel's advance in every era, per the longer ending of Mark; contested by cessationists who limit authenticating signs to the apostolic period.","basis":["Mark 16:17-20 ('these signs will accompany those who believe')","Acts 2:43; 5:12; 14:3 (signs and wonders through the apostles)","2 Corinthians 12:12 ('the signs of a true apostle')","Romans 15:19 (gospel confirmed by the power of signs and wonders)"],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"'Sign' is one of the more stable terms in biblical interpretation: virtually all traditions (Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, and academic biblical scholarship) agree on the core sense of a pointer to divine reality rather than an end in itself, with Johannine usage treated as the theological center. Disagreements are contextual rather than definitional — which category of sign is in view (authenticating miracle, covenant marker, eschatological portent, sacrament, prophetic act) and whether sign-working continues today (continuationist vs. cessationist). The scholarly literature also notes the deliberate Johannine contrast between 'signs' (semeia) and mere 'wonders' (terata): signs demand interpretation and faith, not just amazement. Because the term is genuinely polyvalent across Scripture, an author could plausibly foreground any of the listed senses, but the 'pointer to God's identity and action, especially Jesus' authenticated identity' reading is the recognizable default in commentaries, Bible dictionaries (e.g., entries on semeion), and catechetical teaching."}
